name: Перехресні зв’язки (1)
description:
'Pen', 'attack on a pinned piece' and 'a pinned piece is a poor defender' are forms of pinning that were covered in the previous level.

The above forms were covered separately, but in this lesson they all reappear in a single move. We are introduced to a special form of the pin: the cross pin.

What should you do?

Win material or mate thanks to performing a cross pin.

examples.text:
The black bishop is partially pinned. The bishop cannot move across the a8-h1 diagonal, but action is possible across the a4-e8 diagonal. By attacking the black bishop with a new pawn, white can take advantage of the bishop's vulnerable position.

1.Qe4! pins the bishop (completely), because after 1...Bxb5 the queen is unprotected: 2.Qxb7. Also, white attacks a pinned piece and we can observe that a pinned piece is a poor defender (although the bishop looks at e4, it cannot capture the queen, because then black puts itself in check). White wins material.

This is a cross-pin over diagonals, i.e. a 'pure' cross-pin. In chess literature, this pin is also known as the St Andrew's Cross.

A cross-pin can also be about rows and files:

With 1.Rge1! the rook on e2 is pinned in two ways. If black captures the queen with the rook, a backrank mate follows: 1...Rxd2 2.Re8#. However, getting the rook from the second row is no fun for black either. White captures the queen: 1...Rxe1 2.Qxf2. If black does nothing, on the next move white takes the rook which is attacked twice and only covered once. In short, white wins material!

A cross move over rows and files is known in chess literature as the Maltese Cross.

Note that 1.Rde1 is not good. Black can then capture the rook with check! This leaves white no time to capture the uncovered queen. If white knocks back the rook with the rook, black can use the queen to capture the white queen with check (check again!). This does not give white time to mate on the bottom row. Black stays ahead by a piece.

Finally, a cross pin that goes straight (file or row) and diagonally. An angled cross:

The black queen cannot move off the diagonal b1-h7, because of Qxh7#. The exception is that black can capture the white knight. In this case, capturing on h7 makes little sense for white because the queen is no longer guarded by the knight. However, white can bring a new checkmate threat into the position, so capturing the knight is not an option for black: 1.Rf2!

White attacks the queen and gains material as a result. In fact, moving the queen away always means that black gets checkmated! As many as three of White's pieces are unprotected, but White does not care. If Black takes the knight or the queen, then the checkmate occurs: 1...Qxg5/1...Qxb1 2.Rf8#. If white captures the rook, we see the checkmate close up: 1...Qxf2 2.Qxh7#. Black thus has the choice of being matched or losing a queen. White is winning!

texts: Pieces on the same file, rank, or diagonal offer tactical chances for pins.
